sec.title: Background
sec.p: Diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma (DIPG) is a fatal pediatric brain tumor affecting over 300 children annually in the United States. Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells are a targeted immune effector cell therapy with substantial clinical benefit against hematologic cancers. Against central nervous system (CNS) tumors, CAR T cells targeting B7-H3, a protein highly expressed on DIPG, have rapidly advanced from preclinical studies to clinical trials. BrainChild-03 (NCT04185038), a phase 1 trial of repeatedly delivered intracerebroventricular (ICV) B7-H3-targeting CAR T cells (B7-H3 CAR T cells), demonstrated tolerability and potential efficacy for children and young adults with DIPG. However, clinical benefits were not uniformly seen, and multi-agent treatment strategies may be required against such an aggressive disease. Here, we combined B7-H3 CAR T cells with ONC206, an imipridone molecule also under clinical investigation.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We tested B7-H3 CAR T cells combined with ONC206 across multiple DIPG cell cultures and orthotopic xenograft mouse models.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: B7-H3 CAR T cell monotherapy induced robust cytotoxicity while ONC206 treatment resulted in significant mitochondrial dysfunction against DIPG cells. The combination of low effector-to-target ratios of B7-H3 CAR T cells and IC50 concentrations of ONC206 led to significantly enhanced cytotoxicity in vitro (P < .003) and increased IL-2, IL-29, VEGF-A, and Granzyme B levels. In vivo combinatorial studies of ONC206 and a single ICV dose of B7-H3 CAR T cells extended survival in DIPG xenograft mouse models.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: B7-H3 CAR T cells combined with ONC206 are a feasible and efficacious multi-agent approach against multiple DIPG models.
Keywords: B7-H3, CAR T cell therapy, diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma (DIPG), diffuse midline glioma, H3K27-altered (DMG), ONC206

boxed-text.p: Diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma (DIPG) is a fatal pediatric brain tumor. While B7-H3 CAR T cells have shown tolerability and potential benefit in early trials, combinatorial regimens may be required for consistent cures against this aggressive disease. This study demonstrates that a preclinical therapeutic regimen of B7-H3 CAR T cells with the imipridone ONC206 increases anti-tumor efficacy in vitro and in orthotopic DIPG mouse models. To our knowledge, this is the first study to evaluate ONC206 in combination with CAR T cells. Our findings provide a preclinical roadmap for evaluating small molecules with CAR T cells to interrogate both their combined benefit and the effect of small molecules on T cells themselves. This work offers a biologically-informed, clinically translatable strategy integrating small molecule therapeutics with CAR T cell therapy and supports the development of multi-agent immunotherapy trials for children with DIPG and other high-grade brain and spinal cord tumors.

body.p: Diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma (DIPG) is a fatal pediatric brain tumor most often diagnosed in children between 5 and 10 years of age.1 The prognosis remains dismal, with a median survival under 12 months, largely due to its unresectable location and its resistance to conventional therapies.2 However, recent advances in immunotherapy, particularly chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy, have opened new therapeutic avenues for cancer treatment. In particular, B7-H3, a transmembrane protein involved in regulating T cell response3 has emerged as a promising therapeutic CAR T cell target on DIPG.4–6

Seattle Children’s phase 1 clinical trial (BrainChild-03, NCT04185038) evaluated the safety and feasibility of locoregional B7-H3-targeting CAR T cells (B7-H3 CAR T cells) for DIPG and recurrent pediatric central nervous system (CNS) tumors. This trial demonstrated the tolerability of multiple intracerebroventricular (ICV) doses of B7-H3 CAR T cells at up to 100 million cells/dose given to young children in the outpatient setting.7 While 3 patients were alive beyond 4 years from diagnosis, response to treatment was not uniform, suggesting the potential need for multi-agent therapy.

To improve B7-H3 CAR T cell activity, we explored small-molecule combinations to modulate tumor susceptibility to immunotherapy. Imipridones are pro-apoptotic compounds with a tricyclic core structure targeting dopamine receptor D2 (DRD2) and modulating AKT and ERK signaling pathways.8 More recent studies have shown that imipridones bind to the caseinolytic protease proteolytic subunit (ClpP) and activate the integrated stress response (ISR) cascade.9,10 ONC201, the first-in-class molecule, can cross the blood-brain barrier and has shown activity against several tumor types, including brain cancers.11,12 ONC206, an analog of ONC201 with a greater binding affinity and selectivity,13 follows the same mechanism of action by inducing apoptosis and stress-related signaling pathways.14

Here, we investigate the combinatorial potential of B7-H3 CAR T cells with ONC206. By pairing the tumor-targeting specificity of B7-H3 CAR T cells with the pro-apoptotic and stress-inducing properties of ONC206, this approach aims to enhance antitumor efficacy while maintaining tolerability, supporting the development of rational cellular therapy and drug combinations against DIPG.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: All vendors and catalog numbers are listed in Table S1.

sec.title: Human Specimen and Patient-Derived Cell Cultures
sec.p: PBT-22FH (H3.3 mutant), PBT-24 (H3 wild-type hypermutant), PBT-27FH (H3.1 mutant), and PBT-29FH (H3.3 mutant) were generated from treatment-naïve patient-derived biopsy samples obtained at Seattle Children’s Hospital and established at Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center, as previously described.15 Genetic and molecular characteristics of these models are summarized in Table S2. SU-DIPG-XIII (H3.3 mutant) was autopsy-derived and donated by Dr. Michelle Monje (Stanford University). DIPG models were cultured in NeuroCult NS-A Basal Medium with NS-A Proliferation Supplement (Stemcell Technologies), 40 ng/mL EGF, and 40 ng/mL FGF (PeproTech), along with 2 mM GlutaMax (Gibco). Lenti-X 293T cells, used for CAR lentivirus production, were provided by Prof. Michele Bernasconi and cultured in DMEM medium (Gibco) supplemented with 10% of FBS (Thermofisher). All cell cultures were periodically authenticated by DNA fingerprinting.

sec.title: Lentivirus Production
sec.p: Lentiviruses (LVs) were generated by co-transfecting 5 × 106 Lenti-X 293T cells, seeded onto collagen type I rat tail-coated P10 plates and cultured overnight in DMEM with 10% FBS and GlutaMax. Transfection was performed via calcium phosphate method with 10 µg of psPAX2, 4 µg of pVSV-G, and 10 µg of lentiviral B7-H3 CAR plasmid, as previously described.16 Supernatants were collected 48 hours post-transfection, filtered (0.45 µm), concentrated by overnight centrifugation at 4,000 × g at 4°C, aliquoted, and stored at −80°C.

sec.title: CAR T Cell Manufacturing
sec.p: T cells were isolated from healthy-donor PBMCs (Bloodworks Northwest) via negative selection (EasySep™ isolation kit). Cells were stimulated with anti-CD3/CD28 Dynabeads for 36 hours and transduced at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 5 with titered lentivirus.16 CAR T cells were maintained at 0.8 × 10⁶ cells/mL in RPMI with 10% FBS, GlutaMAX, 5 ng/mL IL-7, and 0.5 ng/mL IL-15, with cell counting performed every other day. After expansion, cells were cryopreserved in CryoStor® CS10 until use.

sec.title: Bioluminescence Survival Assays
sec.p: At day 0, 5,000 iRFP720+ firefly luciferase-positive (fLuc+) tumor cells were seeded in 150 µL of NeuroCult medium (Stemcell) in bioluminescence-compatible 96-well plates. At day 1, 50 µL ONC206 (150 to 300 nM) and/or 50 µL B7-H3 CAR T cells were added at effector-to-target (E: T) ratios of 1:10, 1:4, 1:2, 1:1, 2:1, and 5:1. Mock T cells served as negative controls; medium alone replaced ONC206 or CAR T cells in control wells. For measurements, D-luciferin (30 µg/mL) was added to wells and incubated for 10 min at room temperature before quantification on a SpectraMax iD3 Multi-Mode Microplate Reader (Danaher). Data were analyzed using Excel and GraphPad Prism 10 (La Jolla, CA, USA).

sec.title: Live-Imaging Cytotoxicity Assays
sec.p: For 2- or 7-day assays, 5,000 iRFP720+/fLuc+ tumor cells were seeded at day 0 in black/clear 96-well plates with 150 µL NeuroCult medium. At day 1, 50 µL ONC206 (150 to 300 nM) and/or 50 µL B7-H3 CAR T cells were added at E: T ratios of 1:10, 1:4, 1:2, 1:1, and 5:1. Medium replaced CAR T cells and/or ONC206 in controls. Images were acquired every 4 hours using the Incucyte S3 (Sartorius). Phase-contrast images were normalized to day-0 baselines and analyzed with Incucyte 2022B Rev2 and Graphpad Prism 10.

sec.title: Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assays
sec.p: A total of 50,000 PBT-22FH, PBT-24FH, PBT-27FH, PBT-29FH, or SU-DIPG-XIII cells were seeded in 24-well plates and co-cultured with 250,000 B7-H3 CAR T cells (E: T 5:1) in 1 mL NeuroCult medium. After 24 hours, supernatants were collected and stored at −80°C. Human IL-2, TNF-α, and IFN-γ were quantified by ELISAs according to the manufacturer’s protocols. Data were processed using Microsoft Excel, and figures were generated with GraphPad Prism 10.

sec.title: Annexin-V Assays
sec.p: Early apoptosis was assessed by Annexin-V staining and flow cytometry. DIPG cell cultures (PBT-22FH, PBT-24FH, PBT-27FH, PBT-29FH, SU-DIPG-XIII) and CAR T cells from 3 independent healthy donors were treated for 48 hours with ONC206 (vehicle, 250 nM, or 500 nM). Cells were harvested, washed with PBS, and stained with FITC-Annexin-V antibody in binding buffer following the manufacturer’s protocol. Samples were acquired on Cytoflex (Beckman Coulter) and analyzed using FlowJo (BD). Early apoptosis was quantified as the percentage of Annexin-V-positive cells.

sec.title: Seahorse Assays
sec.p: Oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) were measured using the Seahorse XFe96 Analyzer and the Cell Mito Stress Test Kit (Agilent). PBT-22FH, PBT-24FH, PBT-27FH, PBT-29FH, and SU-DIPG-XIII cells were treated for 48 hours with ONC206 (150 to 300 nM) or vehicle or vehicle containing DMSO. Before measurement, cells were washed and incubated for 1 hour in unbuffered XF Base Medium (Agilent) at 37°C in a CO₂-free incubator. The Mito Stress Test was performed with sequential injections of oligomycin (2 µM), FCCP (2 µM), and rotenone/antimycin A (0.5 µM). Basal respiration, ATP-linked respiration, maximal respiration, spare capacity, coupling efficiency, non-mitochondrial respiration, and ECAR were calculated using Wave Desktop software. Non-mitochondrial OCR (post–rotenone/antimycin A) was subtracted to derive mitochondrial-specific values. Wells with injection failure or aberrant kinetics were excluded. Energy-phenotype assignments (ie “aerobic,” “glycolytic,” “quiescent,” “energetic”) followed Agilent XF Analyzer reference thresholds. All procedures followed the manufacturer’s instructions.

sec.title: Flow Cytometry
sec.p: Surface antigen expression was assessed using the primary antibodies listed in Table S1. T cell phenotyping included CD62L, CD3, CD4, CD8, and CD45RA to define naïve, central-memory, and effector subsets, while LAG-3, PD-1, and TIM-3 were used to assess exhaustion before and after killing assays. Cells were washed twice in flow buffer (PBS + 2% BSA) and incubated for 30 min at room temperature with primary antibodies (1:100), followed by 2 washes before acquisition on a CytoFLEX cytometer (Beckman Coulter). Gating included FSC/SSC, singlets, and CD3 positivity for T cell selection. Transduction efficiency was evaluated 48 hours post-transduction by EGFRt expression relative to untransduced (mock) T cells. B7-H3 surface density was quantified using Quantibrite PE beads (BD). Samples stained with PE-anti-B7-H3 antibody were run alongside beads, and a standard curve was generated to convert MFI into molecules of equivalent PE (MEPE). Intracellular staining to validate target overexpression was performed using the eBioscience Foxp3/Transcription Factor Staining Buffer Set (Thermo Fisher) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Flow cytometry data were analyzed in FlowJo (BD).

sec.title: Multiplex Immunoassays
sec.p: To evaluate cytokine release, 100,000 PBT-27FH and PBT-29FH cells were co-cultured with an equal number of CAR T cells in 24-well plates with ONC206 (250 nM) for 5 days in NeuroCult medium. Supernatants were collected and analyzed using the human cytokine/chemokine 96-plex discovery assay® (Eve Technologies, Calgary, AB, Canada). Cytokine concentrations were quantified and normalized for subsequent analysis. Statistical analyses were performed in R using lme4 and emmeans. A linear mixed-effects model was fitted with log2-transformed cytokine values as the response and cell line, treatment, and cytokine as fixed effects; donor was included as a random intercept. Linear contrasts (eg “ONC206&CAR T vs. CAR T” and “ONC206 vs. vehicle”) were estimated with false-discovery-rate-adjusted p-values.

sec.title: RNA Sequencing
sec.p: For RNA-seq, 100,000 DIPG cells were co-cultured with 100,000 CAR T cells and ONC206 (250 nM) for 5 days in NeuroCult medium. RNA was extracted using the RNeasy Plus Mini Kit (Qiagen) and sent to Novogene for sequencing. FASTQ files were processed using FastP17,18 for adapter trimming and quality filtering, with quality checks performed using FastQC. Reads were pseudoaligned to the human GRCh38 cDNA transcriptome (Ensembl v113)19 using Kallisto (version 0.51.1)20 and summary metrics were reviewed with MultiQC.21 All post-processing steps were run using RStudio (version 2024.12.0 + 467; R Core Team, 2022). Transcripts were imported into R via tximport (version 1.34.0),22 converted to TPM, and normalization using TMM in edgeR (version 4.4.2).23–25 PCA plots were generated using prcomp. Differential expression analysis was conducted with limma (version 3.62.2),26 applying thresholds of FDR < 0.05, counts per million (CPM)≥1 in ≥1 comparator, and Log2(FC)≥2. Gene Ontology overrepresentation analyses of upregulated genes were performed using the PANTHER Classification System (v18.0) with Fisher’s exact test and FDR correction (0.05). Figures were created in GraphPad Prism 10.

sec.title: Drug Combination and Synergy Analyses
sec.p: The combinatorial effects of ONC206 and CAR T cells were evaluated using SynergyFinder 3.0 (https://synergyfinder.fimm.fi). Dose-response matrices were generated for 5 DIPG models (PBT-22FH, PBT-24FH, PBT-27FH, PBT-29FH, SU-DIPG-XIII) after 120-hour co-culture with ONC206 (150 to 500 nM) and CAR T cells at E: T ratios from 0.1:1 to 1:1. Synergy scores were computed using ZIP, Loewe, Bliss, and HSA models, and visualized via SynergyFinder and GraphPad Prism 10. Interactions were classified as synergistic (>10), additive (−10 to 10), or antagonistic (<−10).

sec.title: Surgical Procedure and in Vivo Experimentation
sec.p: Eight-week-old female NOD.Cg-Prkdcscid Il2rgtm1Wjl/SzJ (NSG) mice were housed under pathogen-free conditions at Seattle Children’s Research Institute. All procedures were approved by the IACUC (protocol #IACUC00669). Intracranial SU-DIPG-XIII xenografts were established by injecting 50,000 mCherry/fLuc+ tumor cells at 0.8 mm lateral, 1.5 mm posterior, and 2.5 mm depth relative to lambda. Only animals with confirmed tumor engraftment via rising bioluminescent signal were included. Mice received intracerebroventricular (ICV) injections of 1 × 106 Mock or CAR T cells, and ONC206 was administered orally twice weekly at 50 mg/kg. Intracranial PBT-29FH xenografts were established by injecting tumor fragments at 1 mm lateral, 1 mm posterior, and 2 mm depth relative to lambda. End of study immunohistochemistry confirmed tumor in all enrolled mice. Mice received ICV injections of 2.5 × 105 Mock or CAR T cells, and ONC206 was administered orally twice weekly at 50 mg/kg. For both models, mice were observed for treatment-related toxicity and euthanized upon neurological decline or >20% weight loss.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: Analyses were performed in GraphPad Prism 10. Dose response curves were fitted by nonlinear regression (log[inhibitor] vs. response, 4 parameters). Cell proliferation assays were analyzed using two-way ANOVA with Sidak’s correction. Seahorse data by one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s test. Mouse survival was assessed using Kaplan-Meier curves with log-rank testing; multiple comparisons were adjusted using the Holm-Šidák method. Cox proportional hazards models (Efron method) were used to estimate effect sizes, and β coefficients, hazard ratios, and 95% CIs are reported in Table S3. Animals were randomized to treatment groups, and imaging and bioluminescence quantification were performed blinded. Bar graphs show individual biological replicates with mean ± SD. Sample sizes are provided in figure legends (one mouse = one biological replicate for in vivo studies; for in vitro assays, “n” indicates biological donor replicates unless noted). Statistical significance was defined as ns (P > .05), * (P ≤ .05), ** (P ≤ .01), *** (P ≤ .001), and **** (P ≤ .0001).

sec.title: Illustrations
sec.p: Schemas and illustrations were generated with BioRender.com.

sec.title: On-Target Effector Function of B7-H3 CAR T Cells Against DIPG Models With High Target Expression
sec.p: We first quantified the expression of B7-H3 on treatment-naïve, patient-derived DIPG models (PBT-22FH, PBT-24FH, PBT-27FH, PBT-29FH15,27) and the autopsy-derived SU-DIPG-XIII model. As previously reported,4,5,28,29 all models displayed high surface density, ranging from ∼30,000 to >200,000 molecules per cell, with PBT-24FH showing the highest expression (Figure 1A).

caption.p: B7-H3 expression in DIPG models and efficacy of B7-H3 CAR T cells. (A) Flow-cytometry analysis of B7-H3 surface expression in wild-type PBT-22FH, PBT-24FH, PBT-27FH, PBT-29FH, and SU-DIPG-XIII using a PE-conjugated anti-B7-H3 antibody. All models showed uniformly high B7-H3 expression, and surface copy numbers were quantified using BD Quantibrite beads. (B) Cytotoxicity of B7-H3 CAR T cells against fLuc+/iRFP720+ DIPG cells across multiple effector-to-target (E: T) ratios after 48 hours, measured by luciferase assay and normalized to Mock (UTD) T cells; values represent pooled data from n = 3 independent donors, and PBT-24FH exhibited greater sensitivity to CAR T cell killing, when compared to the other models (P < .001). (C) Live-cell imaging of low-dose B7-H3 CAR T cells (representative donor #1) monitored over time; values were normalized to t = 0 hour and used to define optimal conditions for subsequent ONC206 combination experiments. (D) Quantification of IL-2, IFN-γ, and TNF-α secretion after 24-hour co-incubation of CAR T cells with DIPG models by ELISA; values are pooled from n = 3 independent donors. Statistical significance: ns (P > .05), *(P ≤ .05), **( P ≤ .01), *** (P ≤ .001), **** (P ≤ .0001). All experiments used n = 3 independent donors unless otherwise specified.

sec.p: B7-H3 CAR T cells generated from 3 healthy donors showed consistent transduction and expansion (Figure S1A and B). Across increasing effector-to-target (E: T) ratios, CAR T cells mediated potent cytotoxicity, achieving >50% lysis at 1:1 after 48 hours (Figure 1B). PBT-24FH, the H3 wild-type hypermutant model, was particularly sensitive to CAR T cell treatment, showing ∼40% reduced survival even at the lowest E: T ratio (1:10) and indicating that B7-H3 targeting is effective beyond H3K27-altered tumors (Figure 1B).

To evaluate long-term responses at low CAR T cell doses and identify conditions suitable for drug-combination testing, Incucyte live-imaging assays were performed (Figure 1C). Consistent with previous findings, an E: T ratio of 1:1 confirmed a cytostatic-like effect in most models, while PBT-24FH cells were cleared more rapidly. Of note, higher E: T ratios caused extensive tumor lysis, limiting their suitability for synergy studies; therefore, low E: T conditions were selected for subsequent experiments with ONC206. Cytokine profiling further confirmed CAR T cell activity. After co-culture with DIPG models, B7-H3 CAR T cells released markedly higher IL-2, IFN-γ, and TNF-α than mock T cells, with the strongest response against PBT-24FH (∼1750 pg/mL IL-2, ∼1000 pg/mL IFN-γ, ∼700 pg/mL TNF-α; Figure 1D). Together, these findings validated B7-H3 CAR T cell cytotoxicity and informed selection of optimal low-dose conditions for ONC206 combination testing.

sec.title: ONC206 Shows Limited Effects on CAR T Cell Proliferation
sec.p: To identify drugs suitable for combination with B7-H3 CAR T cells, we evaluated several candidates with reported activity in DIPG models, including marizomib, ONC206, paxalisib, zotiraciclib, everolimus, and conventional chemotherapies (carboplatin, etoposide, vincristine). Marizomib, a proteasome inhibitor, has demonstrated blood-brain barrier penetration.30,31 ONC206, an imipridone derivative of ONC201, has shown enhanced potency against DIPG models, making it a promising therapeutic candidate currently under clinical investigation.13,32 Paxalisib targets the PI3K/mTOR pathway and is investigated in active clinical trials.33–35 Zotiraciclib, a CDK9 inhibitor, displays strong anti-glioma activity, suggesting its potential applicability in treating DIPG.36,37

To assess baseline drug sensitivity, IC50 values were determined after 120 hours of treatment using Cell Titer-Glo assays in 2 representative diffuse midline glioma, H3K27-altered (DMG)/DIPG models, the H3.1-mutant PBT-27FH and the H3.3-mutant PBT-29FH (Figure 2A-C). We next evaluated whether these agents were compatible with B7-H3 CAR T cell therapy. CAR T cells were activated through tumor co-culture before drug exposure, after which compounds were applied at biologically relevant inhibitory doses and CAR T cell expansion was monitored to quantify drug effects following antigen-driven activation.

sec.p: Across the viability curves (Figure 2D and E) and fold-change expansion relative to vehicle-treated CAR T cells (Figure 2F and G), ONC206 combined strong anti-tumor activity with minimal impact on CAR T cell proliferation. In contrast, several other compounds either reduced CAR T cell proliferation or exhibited limited cytotoxicity against DIPG cells. Paxalisib was not further explored due to an ongoing parallel project,35 while marizomib and carboplatin, although not overtly toxic to CAR T cells, were deprioritized because of insufficient potency in the DIPG models tested. Collectively, these results identified ONC206 as the most suitable candidate for subsequent combination studies with B7-H3 CAR T cells.

sec.title: ONC206 Demonstrates Robust Induced Apoptosis across Multiple DIPG Models
sec.p: ONC206, a ClpP agonist and DRD2 antagonist, triggers apoptosis through pathways involving mitochondrial dysfunction and stress response signaling.13,14,38,39 We evaluated its activity across 5 DIPG/DMG models (PBT-22FH, PBT-24FH, PBT-27FH, PBT-29FH, SU-DIPG-XIII), identifying an IC50 range of 217 to 298 nM after 120 hours (Figure 3A), leading to the selection of an average concentration of 250 nM for downstream studies. Parallel experiments in B7-H3 CAR T cells from 3 donors showed a higher IC50 of 357 nM (Figure S1C).

caption.p: ONC206 cytotoxicity and apoptosis induction in DIPG models. (A) Dose-response curves of ONC206 in PBT-22FH, PBT-24FH, PBT-27FH, PBT-29FH, and SU-DIPG-XIII cells following 120 hour of exposure (n = 3 biological replicates). I5C50 values consistently ranged between 217 and 298 nM across models. (B) Early apoptosis measured by Annexin-V flow cytometry after 48 hours of ONC206 treatment at 250 nM or 500 nM (representative of n = 2 independent experiments). (C) Caspase-3/7 activation monitored over 7 days by live-cell imaging (n = 3 biological replicates), showing a peak at ∼120 hours near IC50 doses in most models; SU-DIPG-XIII displayed a delayed and attenuated peak (∼164 hours). (D) Live-cell imaging-based viability analysis (n = 3 biological replicates) confirming ONC206 efficacy at concentrations ≥0.32 μM, with partial resistance at 0.32 μM in PBT-24FH and SU-DIPG-XIII. Representative replicates are shown. (C and D) show the most representative biological replicates.

sec.p: Annexin-V staining at 48 hours revealed a dose-dependent increase in early apoptosis, with more evident effects at 500 nM in PBT-24FH, PBT-27FH, and PBT-29FH (Figure 3B). In contrast, SU-DIPG-XIII showed minimal annexin-V positivity (0.5% at 250 nM; 0.2% at 500 nM), consistent with intrinsic resistance, similar to previously reported ONC201 data implicating cellular reduction-oxidation (redox)/phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) pathway activation in this model.34 Interestingly, Annexin-V staining of CAR T cells showed no early apoptosis even at 500 nM (Figure S1D).

Caspase-3/7 kinetics confirmed a broad apoptotic response. Concentrations ≥1 µM triggered rapid apoptosis, whereas <0.03 µM had minimal effects. ∼IC50 levels (0.32 μM) induced a distinct caspase peak at ∼120 hours across most models, defining this timepoint as optimal (Figure 3C). As previously observed, SU-DIPG-XIII showed a delayed apoptotic peak after ∼168 hours at 0.32 μM, reinforcing its apoptosis-resistant phenotype. Vehicle controls showed negligible activation. ONC206 caused significant cytotoxicity across all cultures, with complete cell death observed within 7 days at ≥0.32 μM (Figure 3D). Importantly, ONC206 doses ≤0.32 µM did not induce caspase-3/7 activation in B7-H3 CAR T cells (Figure S1E), supporting the use of 250 to 300 nM in combination studies.

Transcriptomic profiling further defined ONC206’s apoptotic effects. RNA-seq was performed after 120 hours co-culture with CAR T cells and ONC206 (250 nM) in PBT-27FH and PBT-29FH. All samples produced high-quality transcriptomes with robust human mapping (Figure S2A). PCA showed separation between models along PC1 (57.4%), consistent with their distinct genetic backgrounds, while PC2 (22%) segregated ONC206-treated from vehicle-treated samples, indicating treatment-driven transcriptional divergence (Figure S2B). Differential expression analysis identified 6,953 altered genes in PBT-27FH and 7,404 in PBT-29FH (adjusted P < .05). Applying stringent biological thresholds (log₂FC > 2; CPM > 1) yielded 381 and 390 upregulated genes, respectively (Figure S2C), with 140 shared across both models (Figure S2D). Full lists of differentially expressed genes can be found in Table S4.

Gene ontology (GO) enrichment revealed strong overrepresentation of programmed cell death pathways (GO: 0043067), including positive regulation of apoptotic process (GO: 0043065) and endoplasmic reticulum stress-induced intrinsic apoptosis (GO: 0070059) (Figure S2E). Within GO: 0043065, 37 pro-apoptotic genes were significantly upregulated in at least one model following ONC206 treatment—including ATF3, BBC3, BMF, DDIT3, FOSL1, and TNFRSF10B (DR5)—supporting a consistent apoptotic signature (Figure S2F). Protein validation by flow cytometry confirmed ONC206-induced upregulation of DR5, ATF3, and CHOP (Figure S3A-C). Full gene ontology lists can be found in Table S5.

sec.title: ONC206 Selectively Disrupts Tumor Cell Metabolism While Preserving CAR T Cell Bioenergetics
sec.p: Based on preliminary cytotoxicity results, we next examined the metabolic effects of ONC206 at concentrations near the IC50 (150 to 300 nM). DIPG/DMG models (PBT-22FH, PBT-24FH, PBT-27FH, PBT-29FH, SU-DIPG-XIII) and CAR T cells were treated for 48 hours, and mitochondrial function was assessed using Seahorse Mito Stress Test parameters. At low doses (150 nM), ONC206 already altered metabolic profiles in DIPG cells (Figure 4A). A clear dose-dependent metabolic stress response was observed across all DIPG models (Figures S4 and S5). In contrast, CAR T cell bioenergetics were minimally affected at IC50-range concentrations (Figure 4A). At 250 nM, ONC206 caused near-complete collapse of mitochondrial respiration in tumor cells, reflected by markedly reduced OCR traces (Figure 4A). Fold-change quantification confirmed >90% reduction in basal respiration in DIPG cultures (Figure 4B, P < .0001), consistent with severe mitochondrial dysfunction. ATP-linked respiration and non-mitochondrial respiration were also significantly decreased (P < .05 to P < .001), except in PBT-24FH, which showed partial resistance. Spare respiratory capacity (SRC) was lost across models (Figures S4 and S5). Bioenergetic profiling indicated that ONC206 drove PBT-22FH, PBT-24FH, PBT-27FH, and PBT-29FH into a quiescent phenotype, while SU-DIPG-XIII shifted toward glycolysis (Figure 4C; Figures S4 and S5).40

caption.p: Respiratory response to ONC206 treatment in DIPG models and CAR T cells. (A) Oxygen consumption rate (OCR) profiles of PBT-22FH, PBT-24FH, PBT-27FH, PBT-29FH, SU-DIPG-XIII, and B7-H3 CAR T cells treated with ONC206 at 250 nM for 48 hours, measured over 100 minutes following sequential addition of oligomycin, FCCP, and rotenone/antimycin (n = 2 biological replicates). ONC206 markedly reduced mitochondrial respiration in DIPG cells, whereas CAR T cells showed only limited changes. (B) Quantification of fold-change in maximal OCR and basal respiration relative to vehicle control for all models (representative of n = 2 independent experiments). DIPG cells exhibited a strong reduction in both parameters, while CAR T cells remained largely unaffected. (C) Energy phenotype plots (OCR vs. ECAR) illustrating the metabolic state of each model under vehicle or ONC206 treatment (n = 2). ONC206 shifted DIPG cells toward a quiescent or glycolytic phenotype, whereas CAR T cells maintained an energetic profile, indicating greater metabolic resilience under IC₅0-level ONC206 exposure.

sec.p: On the other hand, CAR T cells displayed a distinct profile, underscoring their resilience to metabolic stress (Figure 4A). Although basal respiration decreased modestly (P < .05), CAR T cells retained >70% of their OCR under ONC206 treatment (Figure 4B). ATP-linked respiration remained largely preserved. Maximal respiration and spare respiratory capacity were maintained (P < .05; Figure S4U), and non-mitochondrial respiration showed only minor reductions (P < .05; Figure S5U-X). Bioenergetic phenotype analyses further confirmed that CAR T cells maintained an energetic phenotype across all conditions, with stable OCR-ECAR balance even at 300 nM (Figure S4X). This preservation of metabolic flexibility highlights the robustness of CAR T cells to ONC206-induced mitochondrial stress.

sec.title: Increased Cytotoxicity of CAR T Cell-Mediated Killing in Combination With ONC206
sec.p: To ensure that combinatorial effects were not driven by altered antigen availability, B7-H3 surface density was quantified after 120 hours of ONC206 exposure. ONC206 did not change B7-H3 surface copy numbers on any models (Figure S1A), indicating that enhanced killing is not due to target modulation. Combination studies were then performed using ONC206 at IC50-range concentrations and low E: T ratios of B7-H3 CAR T cells (1:10 to 1:4) in PBT-22FH, PBT-24FH, PBT-27FH, PBT-29FH, and SU-DIPG-XIII.

Seven-day live-imaging assays revealed a consistent combinatorial killing effect across all models (Figure 5A). Single-agent ONC206 or CAR T cells generally produced cytostatic-like responses relative to mock. In contrast, the combination treatment (green) showed progressively stronger tumor reduction over time, with marked elimination by day 7 in PBT-22FH, PBT-27FH, and PBT-29FH. Luciferase assays at 120 hours supported these findings: while each monotherapy achieved ∼50% killing, the combination produced significantly greater cytotoxicity across the DIPG panel (Figure 5B). These results, confirmed across 3 different CAR T cell donors, support an improved cytotoxic effect mediated by ONC206, which is potentially able to sensitize tumor cells to immune-mediated cytotoxicity, offering the rationale for further preclinical studies.

sec.p: To formally quantify combinatorial effects, 5 × 5 dose-response matrices were generated for all 5 models and analyzed using Bliss, Loewe, HSA, and ZIP reference frameworks (Figures S7A-E, S8A-E). Although synergy scores did not consistently exceed pharmacologic synergy thresholds, the combination reproducibly outperformed either single agent across all models, demonstrating a robust combinatorial benefit.

sec.title: Functional Profile of B7-H3 CAR T Cells Preserved at Low Doses of ONC206
sec.p: To determine whether ONC206 IC50-range concentrations affects CAR T cell effector states, we analyzed T cell phenotypes by assessing the ratios of central memory (TCM), naïve-like (TN), effector (TE), and effector memory (TEM) T cells across 3 donors. CAR T cells were co-cultured with PBT-27FH or PBT-29FH at an E: T ratio of 5:1 in the presence or absence of ONC206 (250 nM). After 5 days, CD3+ CAR T cell phenotype was characterized using CD62L/CD45RA to define subsets. Antigen stimulation by either tumor model produced comparable proportions of TCM (CD62L+/CD45RA−), TE (CD62L−/CD45RA+), and TEM (CD62L−/CD45RA−) across donors, with no differences between ONC206-treated and untreated conditions (Figure 5C). The CD4+/CD8+ ratio similarly remained unchanged in the presence of ONC206 (Figure 5D).

Next, we evaluated the expression of the markers LAG-3, TIM-3, and PD-1 to determine whether ONC206 affects CAR T cell exhaustion. Consistent with the previous results, ONC206 did not increase the frequency of CAR T cells expressing these markers relative to controls (Figure S1F). Together, these data indicate that ONC206 at 250 nM does not alter CAR T cell differentiation status, CD4/CD8 composition, or exhaustion profiles under these conditions.

sec.title: ONC206 IC50 Dose Does Not Impair Cytokine Release in Activated CAR T Cells
sec.p: To assess whether ONC206 affects cytokine secretion, CAR T cells were co-cultured with PBT-27FH or PBT-29FH cells at E: T ratio of 1:1 in the presence or absence of ONC206 (250 nM). After 5 days, supernatants were collected and analyzed using a 96-plex cytokine panel. Linear contrast analyses across 3 T cell donors (eg fold change comparisons referred to as “ONC206 & CAR T vs. CAR T” and “ONC206 vs. vehicle”) showed that ONC206 does not globally suppress CAR T cell cytokine production (Figure 5E,F). While several cytokines, including TRAIL, granzyme A, IL-5, and perforin, were reduced relative to controls, this was offset by significant increases in IL-2, IL-29, IP-10, and VEGF-A (Figure 5E). Importantly, key effector cytokines associated with CAR T cell function—IL-3, IL-6, IL-8, TNF-α, IFN-γ, and granzyme B—remained consistently sustained after ONC206 exposure (Figure 5F).

These findings demonstrate that ONC206 at 250 nM does not substantially affect overall cytokine secretion while selectively modulating specific pathways, maintaining immune functionality. The sustained production of signature CAR T cell cytokines, together with the targeted enhancement of others, supports ONC206 as a well-tolerated agent suitable for combination with B7-H3 CAR T cells.

sec.title: Combination Therapy With ONC206 and B7-H3 CAR T Cells Improves Survival and Maintains Tolerability in Orthotopic DIPG Mouse Models
sec.p: After demonstrating that low doses of ONC206 enhanced B7-H3 CAR T cell-mediated killing in vitro without impairing T cell phenotype, exhaustion, or cytokine release, we tested the combination in 2 orthotopic DIPG mouse models (SU-DIPG-XIII and PBT-29FH). In the SU-DIPG-XIII model, 5 × 104 fLuc+ tumor cells were stereotactically injected into NSG mice (Figure 6A), assigned to 4 groups: Mock T cells + vehicle (control); Mock T cells + ONC206 (ONC206 monotherapy); B7-H3 CAR T cells + vehicle (CAR T monotherapy); or B7-H3 CAR T cells + ONC206 (combination therapy). ONC206 (50 mg/kg) was administered twice weekly from day 3, and CAR T cells were delivered once via ICV on day 7. ONC206 was well tolerated but showed no monotherapy efficacy, with control and ONC206-treated mice reaching endpoint within 12 days post-T cell infusion (median of 15 and 14 days, respectively, Figure 6B). In contrast, low dose CAR T cell alone extended survival (median 25 days), with 2/12 mice surviving until day 40. The combination significantly improved survival (P < .05), delaying tumor progression to at least until day 19; 6 of 12 mice survived beyond day 35 and 3 achieved long-term survival, including one surviving to day 101. Weight data supported good tolerability, with loss occurring only at late disease stages (Figure 6C and D). Hazard ratios for treatment effects were quantified by Cox regression (Table S3).

sec.p: In the PBT-29FH model, tumor fragments were implanted orthotopically, and mouse survival and weight were monitored given the absence of a luciferase reporter. The same treatment groups and dosing schedules were applied, with CAR T cells delivered ICV on day 10 (Figure 6F). ONC206 monotherapy again provided no survival benefit. CAR T monotherapy improved outcomes relative to controls, and the combination further extended survival up to day 85 (Figure 6G). Although not statistically superior to CAR T cells alone, the combination consistently outperformed both monotherapies, mirroring the trend in the SU-DIPG-XIII mouse model. No neurologic toxicity was observed, and weight loss was restricted to advanced disease (Figures 6G and H).

Histological analyses confirmed infiltrative tumors in all groups (H&E staining, Figure S9A), with persistent Ki-67 positivity (Figure S9B). Interestingly, we detected more pronounced cleaved caspase-3 staining in ONC206 and combination groups (Figure S10B and D), and only modest differences in IBA1 and GFAP expression (Figures S11B and D and S12B and D), compared with the respective control groups (Figures S10A and C, S11A and C, and S12A and C), consistent with the limited neuroinflammatory capacity of NSG mice. These findings indicate that ONC206, alone or combined with B7-H3 CAR T cells, does not induce overt damage to normal brain tissue under the tested conditions, while the combination provides superior tumor control and a meaningful survival benefit.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: B7-H3 CAR T cell therapy has emerged as a promising strategy for treating DIPG, offering tumor selectivity, therapeutic tolerability, and potential clinical activity.4,6,41 However, key barriers such as tumor heterogeneity, a suppressive tumor immune microenvironment (TIME), limited CAR T cell persistence, and the infiltrative nature of DIPG continue to constrain therapeutic efficacy, supporting the rationale for combinatorial strategies.

Several aspects of our findings extend prior knowledge on imipridones and B7-H3 CAR T cells. ONC206 has been shown to trigger integrated stress responses and mitochondrial dysfunction in solid tumors,42 while B7-H3 CAR T cells exhibit potent preclinical activity in pediatric cancers.4,6,7,43 Their combined use in DIPG, however, has not been previously evaluated. Our data demonstrates that ONC206 can be combined with B7-H3 CAR T cells without compromising T cell metabolic fitness, phenotype, or cytokine function, establishing ONC206 as a biologically compatible partner for cellular therapies. Most importantly, this study provides the first in vivo evidence that ONC206 enhances CAR T cell-mediated tumor control and prolongs survival in orthotopic models, supporting a novel therapeutic concept integrating targeted metabolic perturbation with antigen-specific immune mechanisms.

We showed that ONC206 robustly induces apoptosis and metabolic collapse in DIPG models, while preserving CAR T cell metabolism and effector functions. At IC50 ONC206 selectively impaired tumor oxidative metabolism but spared CAR T cell respiration. T cell subset distribution, exhaustion marker expression, and CD4/CD8 ratios remained unchanged after prolonged co-culture with ONC206. Cytokine profiling enhanced secretion of IL-2, VEGF-A, IL-29, IP10, IFN-γ, granzyme B, and TNF-α, indicating that ONC206 does not compromise T cell functionality at relevant doses.

Functionally, the combination significantly improved tumor elimination across multiple DIPG cultures, supported by luciferase and live-imaging assays. In vivo, ONC206 did not extend survival as a single agent in these models; however, this outcome may be influenced by the dose, dosing schedule, and tumor characteristics. In alternative settings, it is possible that ONC206 could exhibit greater single-agent anti-tumor activity as a monotherapy. The combination of low doses of B7-H3 CAR T cells combined with ONC206 did yield marked tumor control and significantly extended survival in an aggressive orthotopic DIPG/DMG model, without treatment-related neurologic symptoms or weight loss. The enhanced efficacy is likely mediated by ONC206-driven mitochondrial stress and apoptotic priming in tumor cells, which increases susceptibility to immune-mediated killing. Nevertheless, not all models responded equally, underscoring biological heterogeneity and the need for tailored approaches.

Limitations include the absence of repeated intracranial dosing, a strategy used clinically. Future studies will incorporate early time-point sampling to determine whether ONC206 alters CAR T abundance or activation prior to contraction. Emerging CNS catheter systems44,45 will enable longer-term ONC206 exposure and repeated ICV CAR T cell dosing. Given the limitations of immunodeficient models for studying TIME and neurotoxicity, future studies will utilize immunocompetent models with murine CAR T cells to evaluate ONC206-driven immune modulation and identify inhibitory microenvironmental factors relevant to therapeutic success. While in vivo efficacy may be attenuated relative to in vitro activity, future studies will focus on defining the biologic mechanisms limiting this combination in animal models and identifying strategies to overcome them. These efforts align with ongoing advances in combinatorial therapeutics and optimized strategies.

Ultimately, this work contributes to a broader international effort to develop rational, mechanism-informed therapeutic combinations with higher translational potential.35,46,47 Future studies should define optimal dosing and timing strategies for integrating B7-H3 CAR T cells with ONC206 and assess applicability in other B7-H3-expressing tumors.
